analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 15% excise tax on hedge funds buying single-family homes and ends their landlord tax breaks.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate on February 26, 2026 by a Democrat and a Republican, and was referred to the Finance Committee, where it has not moved since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a 15% tax on the purchase price whenever a large pooled-fund investor — a partnership, corporation, or REIT managing $50 million or more — buys a house or small residential building of 1 to 4 units. The tax disappears only if the buyer occupies the home as their principal residence. It also strips key tax breaks that large institutional landlords use: no deduction for mortgage interest or depreciation on the houses they rent out, and no pass-through income deduction, with the deduction bans starting in 2031 and the surtax arriving after 2035.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary homebuyers competing against Wall Street-backed landlords in the market for houses and small multifamily buildings, and renters in neighborhoods where institutional landlords dominate. The tax makes it 15% more expensive for a hedge fund or REIT to outbid a family for a house, and removing deductions makes holding those homes as rentals less profitable.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 15% excise tax on the purchase price of any 1-to-4 unit residential property acquired by a 'hedge fund taxpayer' — an entity managing pooled investor funds with $50 million or more in assets — unless the property is used as the principal residence of someone with an ownership interest in the buyer.
Exempts tax-exempt nonprofits and companies primarily engaged in building or rehabilitating homes for sale, so homebuilders and mission-driven buyers are not penalized.

Starting after December 31, 2030, denies hedge fund taxpayers in the rental business the mortgage-interest deduction and the depreciation deduction on their single-family rental properties, and after 2035 denies them the qualified business income (pass-through) deduction and adds 5 percentage points to their corporate tax rate.
Applies aggregation rules so affiliated companies under common ownership are treated as one taxpayer, limiting evasion by splitting purchases across subsidiaries.

analysis.who_pays: Large institutional owners of single-family rental homes — hedge funds, private funds, and REITs above the $50 million asset threshold — would pay the 15% purchase tax on new acquisitions, lose major deductions on existing rentals, and face a higher corporate rate after 2035. Some of those costs could be passed to renters through higher rents if funds hold rather than sell.

drawbacks.text: The tax and deduction changes could push up rents in the short run: if institutional landlords keep the houses they own and their costs rise, economists worry some of the cost is passed through to tenants rather than absorbed.

The bill reaches only entities managing pooled investor funds with $50 million or more in assets; smaller landlords and other buyers face no such tax, creating an uneven playing field, and the definition — 'hedge fund taxpayer' despite the title's reference to private equity — may leave some large buyers room to restructure into unregulated forms.
A 15% friction on transactions could reduce market liquidity and make it somewhat harder for any owner, including families, to sell to an institutional buyer if that was their best available bidder.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: making it more expensive for large funds to buy up houses likely helps families compete, but renters living in homes owned by those funds could see costs passed through, and the tax applies unevenly across buyers. The phased timing (deductions after 2030, surtax after 2035) softens the immediate impact. On balance the bill is designed to shift the single-family market away from institutional ownership and toward owner-occupants, with the cost falling on concentrated financial owners.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 26, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley (D-OR) introduced S. 3930, the HOPE for Homeownership Act, on February 26, 2026, joined by one Republican cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation.
As of the latest recorded action, the Finance Committee has taken no further steps on the bill — no hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: large institutional landlords continue to buy and hold single-family rentals with their existing tax advantages intact, while the bill's prospects depend entirely on whether the Finance Committee acts before the Congress ends in January 2027.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 26, 2026 and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan introduction (1 of 55 Senate Republicans).

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship is bipartisan — a Democrat and one of 55 Senate Republicans — but with no committee action, hearing, or vote, no partisan opposition record exists yet.

industries.industry: Institutional owners of single-family rental homes (hedge funds, private funds, and REITs)
industries.note: The bill taxes their acquisitions at 15%, strips their mortgage-interest, depreciation, and pass-through deductions on rental homes, and raises their corporate rate after 2035 — all aimed at making it less profitable for large funds to buy houses that families might buy and to rent them out.

Companies primarily engaged in building or rehabilitating single-family homes for sale are explicitly exempt, so the bill points buyers toward newly built homes and traditional home purchases rather than fund purchases of existing stock.
501(c)(3) nonprofits are exempt from the acquisition tax, preserving their ability to buy homes for community purposes without a 15% penalty.

analysis.trajectory: With a referral to the Senate Finance Committee as the only action and just two sponsors, the bill faces long odds this Congress: the overwhelming majority of Senate bills never get a committee hearing, and Finance's tax docket is typically crowded with larger, leadership-backed legislation. Without many more cosponsors or a push from committee leadership, it is most likely to die in committee, though it could serve as a template or messaging vehicle for housing-affordability legislation.
